newsitem.title: GERMANY: Global airline alliance starts with glitz, promise.
newsitem.headline: Global airline alliance starts with glitz, promise.

text.p: A lot of glitz and little news emerged from the formal launch of a new global airline alliance on Wednesday but industry analysts said the long-standing success of the cooperation far outshines new marketing tricks.

Jumbo jets from the five partner airlines, which include Deutsche Lufthansa AG and United Airlines, were arranged nose-to-nose to form a circle on a tarmac at Frankfurt airport where a tent was constructed for the gala.

The airliners were also adorned with the new symbol of "Star Alliance" -- five three-sided triangles in the shape of a five-sided star -- a bid to create a global image that will further join the carriers but keep their identities.

Other than a statement that Brazilian airline Varig would join the partnership in October, a move also expected, airline executives reaffirmed more carriers would join the partnership, most likely from Africa and Asia.

But analysts said the formal branding effort underscores the success so far of the work between the airlines that began in October 1992 when United and another alliance partner, Air Canada, announced the start of code-share flights.

It also shows how far ahead the carriers are compared with their rivals in building a global network that will be critical for success in the coming years during a time of consolidation, particularly one not solely dependent on transatlantic flights.

The carriers, which also include Thai International Airways and Scandanavian Airlines Systems, have cooperated with one another in recent years with code-sharing flights around the world, combined ground operations, ticketing services and frequent-flier bonus programmes.

The efforts are evident in the numbers: The new alliance, dubbed "The airline network for Earth", has a combined staff of more than 210,000 employees and flights to 578 cities in 106 countries and had combined 1996 revenues of $42 billion.
The airlines together also carried 174 million passengers around the world to nearly 578 cities in 106 countries and want five to six percent annual growth in passenger travel volumes.
"Lufthansa and the others are well placed for the future and that is the key message people should draw from this announcement," said Chris Tarry, an industry analyst at Kleinwort Benson in London.
Analysts said the alliance will now focus on linking up additional partners in the Asia-Pacific region, with Hong Kong-based Cathay Pacific emerging as a top pick.
"The race is on to find partners in Asia and they should find someone rather soon," said Peter Seppelfricke at MM Warburg Investment Research in Hamburg.
Alliance chiefs would not be drawn on the possibility of Cathay joining the alliance or other potential choices, such as Japan Airlines and Air China.
"Looking to the future of the alliance, we are hopeful there will be other airlines in that region who join," Lufthansa chief executive Juergen Weber told reporters.

But the push to Asia will be critical since the alliance forsees no regulatory complications -- a problem the rival partnership between American Airlines and British Airways has faced for nearly a year.

United took another poke at American on Wednesday when UAL Corp chief executive Gerald Greenwald said he was still opposed to the American-British Airways pact, which American said on Tuesday may soon get British government approval.
"There's a misconception about what we are doing compared to what American is proposing to do. There's only similarity and it's the word 'alliance'. Beyond that, we part company," Greenwald said.
